The Twinspot damselfish Chrysiptera biocellata is a small yet robustly built coral reef dweller that exhibits a distinct life-history pattern typical of many pomacentrids. Field surveys indicate that individuals attain a maximum adult body length of 12.5 centimeters [Li = 12.5 centimeters], a size that is modest relative to other damselfish species but well suited to their territorial, benthic lifestyle. Across multiple sampling events on the Great Barrier Reef, researchers have noted that the onset of sexual maturation begins when fish reach a standard length of 5 centimeters [Lp = 5 centimeters], at which point individuals typically weigh approximately 2.9 grams [Wwp = approximately 2.9 grams]. This combination of size and mass at maturity reflects a strategy that prioritises early reproduction, a common trait among small-bodied species that face high predation pressure as recruits. In the same thermal regime typical of shallow lagoon habitats, where water temperatures average 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C], the development of newly hatched larvae proceeds rapidly, with the prolarval stage beginning just 8 days [ab = 8 days] after fertilisation.

Reproductive output in Chrysiptera biocellata is relatively modest when compared to some larger, more fecund pomacentrids but is nonetheless notable given the species’ small body size. At a stable water temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C], each mature female is capable of producing approximately 2,000 eggs per year, which corresponds to a maximum daily reproduction rate of about 5 eggs per day [Ri = about 5 eggs per day] during peak spawning periods. The rate of clutch deposition, averaging roughly 1 spawning event every 3 days [F_R_i = roughly 1 spawning event every 3 days], suggests that females are reproductively active throughout much of the year. Lifetime fecundity is thus constrained less by physiological limits and more by the relatively short reproductive lifespan of the species. This high-frequency spawning strategy is consistent with the findings reported for the congener Dascyllus aruanus, from which the estimate for the maximum reproductive rate was originally derived under similar thermal conditions.

Hatchling mass in the Twinspot damselfish is exceedingly small, a feature that reflects the energetic constraints of producing numerous pelagic eggs. The wet weight of a newly emerged yolk-sac larva is just 0.000091 grams [Wwb = 0.000091 grams], a value that aligns closely with data reported for the related Hawaiian species Dascyllus albisella, from whose egg dimensions (0.7 millimeters long and 0.5 millimeters wide) this estimate was originally extrapolated. Following eclosion, the lecithotrophic larvae rely entirely on their endogenous yolk reserves for sustenance, a period that lasts until the mouth opens and first exogenous feeding commences. At the typical ambient temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C] maintained in laboratory rearing trials, the hatching event occurs reliably after an incubation period of 8 days [ab = 8 days]. This rapid embryogenesis is advantageous in shallow, predator-rich environments where prolonged egg exposure would elevate mortality risk.

The ultimate body mass attained by a fully grown adult of Chrysiptera biocellata has been calculated from length-weight regressions specific to this species. The asymptotic wet weight is 44.6 grams [Wwi = 44.6 grams], a value derived from the relationship W = 0.02344 × L²⁹⁹ applied to individuals of maximum size. This mass is roughly fifteen times greater than the weight recorded at puberty, underscoring the considerable scope for post-maturation somatic growth. In contrast, the corresponding wet weight at birth is less than one ten-thousandth of the adult mass, highlighting the extreme vulnerability of the early life stages. The maximum recorded longevity for this species, based on tag-recapture data collected from a protected lagoon population, is 6 years [am = 6 years] when assessed at the local mean annual temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C]. This lifespan is typical for a small-bodied pomacentrid and allows for multiple reproductive seasons.

An integrative view of the life history of Chrysiptera biocellata reveals a tightly orchestrated sequence of size- and age-dependent transitions. The species becomes reproductively mature at a body length of 5 centimeters [Lp = 5 centimeters], a standard measure that coincides with a wet body weight of 2.9 grams [Wwp = 2.9 grams] in field-caught specimens. From that point onward, adult females can sustain an annual egg output of approximately 2,000 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 2,000 eggs per year] under the consistently warm conditions of their tropical environment. The trade-off between investing in further somatic growth versus gamete production is evident in the magnitude of the mass increase from maturity to the asymptotic mass of 44.6 grams [Wwi = 44.6 grams]. Ultimately, the species’ entire reproductive schedule is compressed within a maximum lifespan of 6 years [am = 6 years], a duration that is brief compared to many larger reef fishes but entirely sufficient for a small, fast-living damselfish to complete numerous breeding cycles at a temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C].
